extracted.intended_audience: high-school students and math-competition contestants (IMO) and their teachers
extracted.subtask_description: Solve and construct classical Euclidean geometry problems (constructions, minimality, reconstructions) using transformation-geometry tools (reflections, rotations, homotheties, shears) and elementary facts; typical audience is contest students and instructors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct perpendicular to a line through a point P (case analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different constructions are required depending on the location of P relative to the given circle/line: P inside the circle, P on the circle, or P on the line AB. The text gives explicit constructions for each case (use of orthocenter when P inside; choose a point Q outside and use perpendiculars and reflections when P lies on the circle; draw two perpendiculars and use a shear when P lies on AB).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For P inside the circle: draw AC and BD so their intersection H is the orthocenter of triangle ABP, hence PH ⟂ AB. For P on the circle: pick Q outside, drop perpendicular from Q to AB meeting circle at R,S; reflect P using R,S by drawing SP meeting AB at T and RT meeting circle to obtain the reflected point P'; then PP' ⟂ AB. For P ∈ AB: draw two perpendiculars to AB meeting circle in S,S' and use SP and S'P to locate points T,T'; use a shear with fixed line SS' to map T'R to RT and argue via equal-area trapezoids that P and its image are equidistant from S'Q, hence PP' ⟂ AB. The full case-split and procedure are given and should be followed exactly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal-number construction objective (minimize lines/circles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some problems explicitly require constructions using the minimal number of auxiliary elements (lines, circles or segments). Example: Problem 9 asks to construct the perpendicular to a given line through P using as few lines as possible (circles or segments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text presents a construction that uses one circle and two straight lines (instead of the classical construction that uses more). General guidance: look for transformations (e.g., draw circle with center Q through P, use diameter RQ etc.) that reduce the number of elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reflections to minimize perimeter (reflection trick)
rubrics_metrics.description: To construct a triangle ABC of minimum perimeter with B and C on the legs of a given angle and A fixed inside, reflect A across the legs to points M,N; then the segment MN intersects the legs at the optimal B and C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard reflection method for shortest-path/perimeter problems: reflect the fixed point across boundary lines and join the reflected points; the intersections with the boundary give the minimizing points. The text gives the inequality argument comparing any other choice B1,C1 to show minimality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowed-tool constraints (ruler-only / straightedge-and-compass)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some constructions are constrained to special toolsets: problems explicitly mark 'Solve by ruler!' or 'By ruler only!' or allow circles/segments and straight lines; the allowed toolkit affects technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a problem stipulates 'ruler only', use projective/ruler-only constructions (e.g., midpoint of parallel segments, parallels through center). When straightedge-and-compass is allowed, use standard compass constructions and reflections. Follow the stated tool restriction exactly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of homothety (centered similarity) to map circles/points
rubrics_metrics.description: Homothety is used to map one circle to another or to map points along concentric structures; examples include mapping ω to ω' with center A to relate arcs, mapping a chain of tangent circles Ci to Ci+1 via homotheties Ti(λi), and composing them to analyze the net effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply homothety with identified centers to map circles or chords; compositions of homotheties are used to deduce global behavior (e.g., product maps C1 to itself, giving identity for even n and half-turn for odd n). Use these mappings to transform difficult geometric loci into simpler ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of rotation compositions and their consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Compositions of rotations (e.g., 60° rotations, 90° rotations) are used to obtain half-turns or other mappings that yield constructions or angle relations (e.g., a composition of three 60° rotations can be a half-turn; two successive 90° rotations give a half-turn mapping a point to another).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you can express a mapping as a product of rotations, compute the net rotation angle and center from composition rules. The text uses this to show, for example, that certain midpoints or images give an isosceles right triangle or to locate centers of symmetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of translations and shear transformations in constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Translations and shears are introduced as legitimate geometric operations: e.g., translate DA to AA1 or use a shear with fixed line SS' to map one segment to another; shears preserve areas and map lines to lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use translations to place segments in convenient positions or to reduce a construction to a standard one. Use shears where area-preservation arguments simplify perpendicularity or equidistance conclusions (as in the construction when P ∈ AB). Explicitly note that shears map trapezoids and preserve area relationships used in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing quadrilaterals/triangles from partial data (reconstruction problems)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several problems require reconstructing a polygon from partial information (e.g., from sides and the median joining midpoints of AB and CD; reconstruct ABC from vertices of exterior regular triangles; reconstruct quadrilateral from midpoints of sides with equal side-length constraints).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common techniques: reflect the figure at known midpoints or centers, apply translations/homotheties to recover original vertices, and use the given metric relations (equal sides, medians) to locate unknowns. The text gives stepwise strategies: reflect ABCD at M to obtain ABD'C' and use translations to construct A1N1N etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area-based arguments and invariance under transformations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use area comparisons preserved by certain transformations (shears, translations) to deduce equal altitudes or perpendicularity. Example: two trapezoids having the same area under a shear imply equidistance properties leading to perpendicularity conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a construction uses a shear or translation, compare areas of corresponding figures (triangles, trapezoids). Equal base and area imply equal altitude; use that to deduce equidistance or orthogonality as required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing perpendiculars and orthocenters via transformation composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Orthocenter properties (intersection of altitudes) and compositions of reflections are used to deduce perpendicular directions: e.g., drawing AC and BD whose reflections are perpendicular to BP and AP yields H as orthocenter of triangle ABP and PH ⟂ AB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit the fact that certain reflected lines become altitudes in a constructed triangle; identify intersections of these auxiliary lines as orthocenters to obtain the desired perpendiculars without directly constructing the altitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Square and parallel-pair constructions from collinear points
rubrics_metrics.description: Given four collinear points A,B,C,D on a line, construct through A,B a pair of parallels (a,b) and through C,D another pair (c,d) so that (a,b) ∪ (c,d) form a square P Q R S (Problem 10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The construction uses pairs of parallels through specified points; use angle-bisector and semicircle-center arguments as indicated in the text to locate the required parallels and ensure a square results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem classification and expected methods for competition geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: The text states that classical Euclidean geometry is central to competitions (e.g., IMO typically includes two geometry problems) and that methods may include vectors, complex numbers, or transformation geometry, but usually require ingenuity and a few elementary facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For contest-level geometry expect a mixture of: (1) elementary synthetic arguments, (2) transformation-based shortcuts (reflections, rotations, homotheties), and (3) occasional algebraic (vector/complex) approaches. Aim to identify the 'right idea' quickly; many 'easy' problems become trivial once the proper transformation is seen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of midpoints/medians and centroid relationships for area and construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Midpoints and medians are used both for construction tasks (e.g., construct triangle from medians; reconstruct a figure from midpoints) and for area relationships (medians partition triangle area into six equal parts; area of triangle from medians is 3/4 of original).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply standard centroid/median facts (equal-area partitions, scaling relations under dilation about a vertex) to transform median data into side-length constructions. The text includes explicit construction recipes using reflections and stretches to obtain triangles from given medians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locus and extremal constructions: reflect, rotate, or use tangent/homothety
rubrics_metrics.description: Many problems ask for loci or extreme positions (e.g., locus of midpoints of XY where X ∈ C1, Y ∈ C2; extreme positions of a rocker in a four-bar linkage). The text prescribes techniques like homothety composition, tangent constructions, and reflecting points to convert locus problems into linear/rotational ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate locus questions into transformation language: identify invariants under mapping (angle, distance ratio), compose homotheties/rotations to find net effect, or reflect to reduce to straight-line intersection problems. Use tangency/homothety centers for circle-locus problems.
